course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments before 1607 provides the most relevant context for English interest in founding colonies in North America?
choices: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680, which convinced English leaders that Spain could be driven out of North America
The Louisiana Purchase, which opened vast western lands to English settlers and merchants
England's naval victory over the Spanish Armada in 1588, which weakened Spain's naval dominance
The French founding of Quebec in 1608, which showed that colonies in North America could be profitable
questions.explanation: The defeat of the Armada in 1588 reduced Spain's naval dominance and made English leaders more willing to challenge Spain in the Americas.
choiceExplanations: The Pueblo Revolt came decades after English colonies began, so it cannot be context from before 1607.
The Louisiana Purchase occurred in 1803, long after the founding of English colonies.
The defeat of the Armada in 1588 reduced Spain's naval dominance and made English leaders more willing to challenge Spain in the Americas.
Quebec was founded after the start of English colonization and cannot be context from before 1607.
questions.distinguisher: Both the Pueblo Revolt and the Armada's defeat involve Spain, but only the Armada's defeat came before 1607.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes a difference between Spanish and French goals in North America?
choices: Spain sought trade partnerships for furs, while France sought to extract wealth and convert Native peoples
Spain sought to extract wealth and convert Native peoples, while France sought trade partnerships for furs
Spain sought large farming settlements of European families, while France sought silver from Native mines
Spain sought to avoid contact with Native peoples, while France sought to rule them through military force
questions.explanation: Spain built institutions to extract wealth and convert Native peoples, while France built a small colony that depended on trade alliances for furs.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the two empires; Spain used conquest and missions, and France relied on the fur trade.
Spain built institutions to extract wealth and convert Native peoples, while France built a small colony that depended on trade alliances for furs.
Spanish colonies depended on Native labor and tribute, and French colonies were small trading posts.
Spain governed Native peoples directly, and France worked through alliances.
questions.distinguisher: The near miss has the two empires' goals reversed.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a similarity among the colonial goals of Spain, France, the Netherlands, and England in North America?
choices: Each sought economic benefit from its colonies, such as wealth, furs, or profit from agriculture
Each sent large numbers of European families to settle permanently on farms and in towns along the coast
Each made converting Native peoples its primary reason for settling in North America
Each avoided armed conflict with American Indians in order to protect its trade and its settlers
questions.explanation: All four empires hoped their colonies would produce wealth, though they pursued it in different ways.
choiceExplanations: All four empires hoped their colonies would produce wealth, though they pursued it in different ways.
Only England did this on a large scale; the French and Dutch colonies had relatively few settlers.
Spain emphasized conversion, but the Dutch and English colonies focused on trade or farming.
Every empire fought with American Indian nations at times.
questions.distinguisher: Only England sent large numbers of families, so the near miss describes a difference, not a similarity.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains how the Protestant Reformation provides context for English colonization?
choices: Protestant leaders ended Spanish colonization, which left North America open to English settlers
Protestant leaders banned English subjects from leaving England, which forced colonization by the Crown
Protestant leaders asked French missionaries to establish colonies in Virginia and New England
Religious conflict led groups such as Puritans and Separatists to seek places to worship as they chose
questions.explanation: Religious divisions after the Reformation led dissenters such as Puritans and Separatists to look for places to worship freely.
choiceExplanations: Spain continued to colonize in the Americas after the Reformation.
English migrants left voluntarily, and the Crown did not require colonization.
French missionaries worked in New France, not in English colonies.
Religious divisions after the Reformation led dissenters such as Puritans and Separatists to look for places to worship freely.
questions.distinguisher: The Reformation did affect Spain, but it did not end Spanish colonization.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why competition among European powers increased conflict in North America?
choices: Rival empires competed for land and furs, but American Indian nations stayed neutral in their disputes
Rival empires competed for land, furs, and fishing grounds and drew American Indian nations into their rivalries
Rival empires signed treaties that divided North America, and Native nations resisted the division
Rival empires competed over religion alone, and economic motives played little part in their conflicts
questions.explanation: Competition for land, furs, and fishing grounds led European powers to fight one another and to bring Native allies into their wars.
choiceExplanations: Native nations frequently allied with Europeans against their own rivals.
Competition for land, furs, and fishing grounds led European powers to fight one another and to bring Native allies into their wars.
The empires did not divide North America by treaty during this period.
Competition over furs, land, and trade was central.
questions.distinguisher: Native nations often joined European conflicts to advance their own interests, so neutrality does not describe the pattern.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why British colonies in different regions developed different economies?
choices: The British government assigned each region a single crop in order to avoid competition among colonies
American Indian nations required each region to produce a specific product in exchange for trade
Differences in environment and resources made some products, such as tobacco or grain, more profitable than others
Spanish officials taught colonists in each region which crops would grow best in the local soil
questions.explanation: Different climates and soils favored different products, so colonies specialized in what their land could produce.
choiceExplanations: Colonists chose crops based on local conditions; Parliament did not assign them.
Native nations did not set crops for colonial regions.
Different climates and soils favored different products, so colonies specialized in what their land could produce.
Spain did not instruct English colonists in agriculture.
questions.distinguisher: Parliament did regulate trade, but colonists, not officials, chose crops according to what the environment allowed.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a major reason many English people migrated to North America in the early 1600s?
choices: A mix of economic hardship, hope for land and prosperity, and religious dissent at home
An English law granting every migrant free land and a seat in the colonial government
Royal orders requiring all unemployed workers to move to the colonies at the Crown's expense
Spanish invitations offering English Protestants safe passage and land in Florida
questions.explanation: English migrants left because of economic pressures, hope of land and mobility, and religious conflict.
choiceExplanations: English migrants left because of economic pressures, hope of land and mobility, and religious conflict.
No law granted every migrant land and a seat in government.
Migration was mostly voluntary and financed by migrants or companies.
Spain was England's rival, and it did not invite English Protestants to settle.
questions.distinguisher: The near miss imagines a single government program, but migrants came for varied reasons, often at their own cost.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The founding of Jamestown in 1607 is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: The Pueblo Revolt, which forced Spain to withdraw from North America and open lands to English settlers
French success in the fur trade, which made English leaders abandon plans for colonies in North America
The Great Awakening, which encouraged English ministers to establish colonies for religious revival
English efforts to compete with Spain by establishing colonies financed by joint-stock companies
questions.explanation: English leaders hoped colonies would bring wealth and challenge Spain, and joint-stock companies like the Virginia Company pooled money for the venture.
choiceExplanations: The Pueblo Revolt came in 1680 and did not remove Spain from North America.
English leaders continued to plan colonies and, in 1607, founded Jamestown.
The Great Awakening began in the 1730s, long after Jamestown.
English leaders hoped colonies would bring wealth and challenge Spain, and joint-stock companies like the Virginia Company pooled money for the venture.
questions.distinguisher: The near miss uses a real Spanish defeat but places it decades after Jamestown.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.
